question: Why do commercial transport aircraft use 115V AC electrical power at 400 Hz instead of 50 Hz or 60 Hz?
options: 400 Hz generators and transformers require much smaller, lighter magnetic iron cores
400 Hz travels much further over long cables with zero voltage drop
400 Hz prevents static electricity from building up on the fuselage skin
400 Hz can be stored directly inside lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries
explanation: Higher alternating current frequency allows magnetic cores in generators and transformers to be roughly one-third to one-fourth the weight of 50/60 Hz units without reaching magnetic saturation.

question: What is the primary purpose of an Integrated Drive Generator (IDG) on an aircraft engine?
options: To convert 28V DC battery power into 115V AC power
To convert variable engine gearbox RPM into a constant generator speed for fixed 400 Hz output
To start the main engine electrically without using APU bleed air
To regulate cabin pressurization outflow valves during climb
explanation: An IDG combines a Constant Speed Drive (CSD) and an AC generator in a single housing so that variable engine N2 speed is converted into a constant RPM, maintaining a steady 400 Hz output frequency.

question: If an Integrated Drive Generator (IDG) is disconnected in flight due to high oil temperature, how is it reconnected?
options: It automatically reconnects once the oil cools below 100°C
By pulling and resetting the IDG circuit breaker on the overhead panel in flight
It can only be mechanically reset on the ground by maintenance personnel with engines shut down
By cycling the APU generator switch off and on
explanation: Disconnecting an IDG mechanically separates the drive clutch inside the unit. It cannot be reconnected in flight and must be reset manually on the ground via the reset ring on the IDG housing with the engine stopped.

question: What device converts 115V AC into 28V DC on a commercial aircraft?
options: Static Inverter
Transformer Rectifier Unit (TRU)
Constant Speed Drive (CSD)
Bus Tie Contactor (BTC)
explanation: A Transformer Rectifier Unit (TRU) steps down 115V AC to 28V AC using a transformer and converts it into 28V DC using a full-wave rectifier.

question: What is the role of the Static Inverter in an aircraft electrical system?
options: It converts 28V DC from the batteries into 115V 400 Hz AC for essential instruments during an emergency
It discharges static electricity from the trailing edge of the wings
It converts 115V AC into 28V DC to charge the main batteries
It connects the Ground Power Unit (GPU) to the service bus
explanation: When normal AC generators are lost, the Static Inverter converts 28V DC battery power into 115V 400 Hz single-phase AC to power the AC Essential Bus.

question: Why are transport-category aircraft tyres inflated with dry nitrogen instead of regular compressed shop air?
options: Nitrogen is 50% lighter than air, reducing landing gear retraction loads
Nitrogen eliminates moisture that freezes at altitude and keeps oxygen below 5% to prevent internal tyre auto-ignition
Nitrogen reacts chemically with rubber to make the tread wear slower on concrete
Nitrogen expands three times faster under heat to cushion hard landings
explanation: Dry nitrogen contains zero moisture (preventing ice in valve cores at -55°C) and is an inert gas that prevents volatile rubber gases from auto-igniting or feeding a brake fire if thermal fusible plugs melt.

question: What is the purpose of thermal fusible plugs installed in aircraft main landing gear wheel rims?
options: To lock the wheel rim halves together if a bolt shears
To melt at a calibrated temperature and deflate the tyre safely before extreme brake heat causes a violent tyre explosion
To measure carbon brake wear during the walkaround inspection
To bleed off excess hydraulic fluid pressure in the brake pistons
explanation: Fusible plugs contain a low-melting-point eutectic alloy core that melts if brake heat becomes excessive (such as after a Rejected Takeoff), releasing nitrogen pressure smoothly rather than letting the tyre burst.

question: On an Airbus A320, what is the maximum brake temperature limit above which takeoff is normally prohibited (with brake fans off)?
explanation: On the A320 family, brake temperatures must be at or below 300°C (with brake fans off) prior to takeoff to prevent retracting an overheated wheel/brake assembly into a confined wheel well with hydraulic lines and tyres.

question: What causes the primary wear on Carbon-Carbon aircraft brake discs during routine airline operations?
options: Only maximum-effort rejected takeoffs
Rainwater washing over the discs on wet runways
The total number of brake pedal applications (especially light taxi snubbing), rather than purely braking force
Aerodynamic drag while the landing gear is extended on approach
explanation: Unlike steel brakes where wear is strictly proportional to kinetic energy absorbed, carbon brake wear is heavily driven by the number of mechanical engagements (pedal applications) during taxi.
source: Airbus Flight Operations Briefing Notes: Braking Systems

question: What is the purpose of the 'Nose Wheel Steering Bypass Pin' inserted by ground crew before pushback?
options: It locks the nose gear up-lock hook so the gear cannot retract on the ground
It mechanically/hydraulically isolates nosewheel steering hydraulics so the tow tug can turn the nosewheel beyond normal steering angles without damaging actuators
It disconnects the cockpit rudder pedals from the tail rudder
It applies the emergency parking brake if the towbar shears
explanation: The steering bypass pin places the nosewheel steering hydraulic loop into bypass mode, allowing the pushback tug to pivot the nosewheel freely without fighting pressurized hydraulic steering actuators.
source: AMM ATA 09 / ATA 32 Towing and Taxiing

question: Inside a landing gear shock-absorber strut (Oleo Strut), which two substances work together to absorb impact energy and support the aircraft?
options: Compressed dry nitrogen gas and mineral hydraulic fluid (MIL-PRF-5606 / 83282)
Compressed shop air and heavy gear grease
Liquid oxygen and purple Skydrol fluid
Steel coil springs and water-glycol mixture
explanation: An oleo-pneumatic shock strut forces hydraulic oil through a Metering Orifice to absorb the kinetic energy of touchdown impact, while compressed dry nitrogen gas acts as the elastic spring supporting the aircraft during taxi.

question: Why are commercial aircraft tyres moulded with straight circumferential 'rib' grooves rather than car-style cross-cut tread blocks?
options: Straight grooves are cheaper to cut by hand at the airport
Straight ribs channel water away to prevent hydroplaning while resisting the extreme 200-knot centrifugal and spin-up shear forces that would tear tread blocks off
Cross-cut tread blocks would jam inside the wheel well doors during retraction
Aircraft wheels have electric drive motors that don't require lateral grip
explanation: Aircraft wheels are unpowered, free-rolling tyres that touch down at 140–170 knots. Straight rib grooves provide directional lateral stability and water evacuation without individual blocks chunking off under high-speed shear.

question: Why is synthetic Phosphate-Ester hydraulic fluid (such as Skydrol) used in commercial airliners instead of red petroleum mineral oil?
options: It is completely non-toxic and gentle on bare skin and paint
It is fire-resistant and self-extinguishing if a 3,000 PSI pinhole leak sprays mist onto hot brakes or engine ducts
It freezes at 0°C to seal leaks automatically at cruise altitude
It can be mixed in any ratio with engine oil and jet fuel
explanation: Phosphate-ester fluid has a very high auto-ignition temperature (>500°C) and resists flame propagation if a high-pressure 3,000 PSI line ruptures into a fine aerosol mist near hot components.

question: Which type of synthetic rubber seal material is compatible with Phosphate-Ester (Skydrol) hydraulic systems?
options: Natural latex rubber
Standard Nitrile (Buna-N)
EPDM (Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer)
Neoprene sponge
explanation: Phosphate-ester hydraulic fluids require EPDM (or PTFE/Teflon) seals; installing standard nitrile (Buna-N) seals meant for mineral oil will cause the seals to swell, soften, and disintegrate.

question: Why are hydraulic reservoirs on transport aircraft pressurized (typically to ~40–50 psi with bleed air)?
options: To cool the hydraulic fluid below -20°C in flight
To prevent pump cavitation and fluid foaming at high altitude where ambient atmospheric pressure is very low
To push the landing gear down if the gravity extension handle jams
To operate the passenger cabin doors when the aircraft is parked
explanation: Pressurizing the hydraulic reservoir ensures a positive head of fluid enters the high-speed engine-driven and electric pumps at high altitude, preventing dissolved air from bubbling out and causing destructive pump cavitation.

question: What is the function of a 'Hydraulic Fuse' installed in a brake or leading-edge slat supply line?
options: It melts if the hydraulic fluid temperature exceeds 120°C
It senses an abnormally high flow rate caused by a ruptured downstream pipe and slams shut to prevent losing the entire system's fluid
It filters microscopic metal particles out of the return line
It converts 3,000 psi pressure down to 500 psi for cabin gauges
explanation: A hydraulic fuse measures volumetric flow or pressure drop; if a downstream line is severed (for example, by a tyre burst in the wheel well), the sudden surge in flow closes the fuse and preserves the main hydraulic reservoir.

question: How is cabin altitude (cabin pressurization) actively controlled during normal flight?
options: By turning the engine bleed air compressors on and off every two minutes
By modulating the position of the motorized Outflow Valve(s) to vary how fast conditioned air escapes overboard
By pumping pure oxygen from high-pressure cylinders into the cabin ducts
By inflating rubber bladders inside the fuselage sidewalls
explanation: Conditioned bleed air is supplied continuously into the cabin by the ECS Packs, while the Cabin Pressure Controller modulates the Outflow Valve(s) near the aft belly to regulate the rate of air escaping.

question: In an aircraft Air Conditioning Pack, what is the role of the Air Cycle Machine (ACM)?
options: It burns a small amount of jet fuel to warm the cabin during polar flights
It compresses hot engine bleed air, cools it across ram-air heat exchangers, and expands it across a turbine to drop its temperature dramatically
It adds humidity to the cockpit windshields to prevent static
It pumps lavatory waste into the aft holding tank
explanation: The Air Cycle Machine (ACM) uses a compressor, ram-air heat exchangers, and an expansion turbine on a common shaft to refrigerate +200°C engine bleed air down to near 0°C without heavy liquid chemical refrigerants.

question: What does pressing the guarded 'DITCHING' pushbutton on the Airbus A320 overhead pressurization panel do?
options: It fires the emergency evacuation slides while the aircraft is still in the air
It dumps all wing fuel overboard in 90 seconds
It closes the Outflow Valve, ram-air inlet, avionics ventilation valves, and pack flow valves below the waterline so the fuselage floats
It detaches the engine pylons upon water impact
explanation: The DITCHING switch sends a close signal to all valves and openings below the fuselage waterline (outflow valve, pack inlets, extract valves) to make the lower hull as watertight as possible for a water landing.

question: Why do cabin air conditioning vents suddenly go quiet right before main engine start at pushback?
options: The pilots turn off all electrical buses to protect the cockpit screens
The Pack Flow Control Valves close automatically so 100% of APU bleed air pressure is routed to the engine Air Turbine Starters
The cabin Outflow Valve opens fully to depressurize the cargo hold
The recirculation HEPA filters run a reverse self-cleaning cycle
explanation: Starting a large turbofan requires maximum pneumatic pressure and airflow from the APU. Closing the ECS Pack valves ensures all APU bleed air is directed to the starter motor.

question: Why are commercial aircraft designed to store fuel inside the wings AND burn the Center Wing Tank before the Wing Tanks?
options: Fuel in the wings is closer to the cockpit gauges for more accurate readings
Keeping fuel weight distributed out in the wings counteracts upward aerodynamic lift ('Wing Bending Relief'), reducing structural stress at the wing roots
Wing tank fuel is colder, so burning it first would freeze the engine fuel nozzles
The center tank has no fuel boost pumps and relies on gravity alone
explanation: In flight, the wings lift the heavy fuselage hung in the center. Keeping fuel weight out in the wings for as long as possible acts downward against aerodynamic lift, relieving upward bending stress on the main wing box spars.

question: What keeps Jet A-1 fuel from freezing solid during a 12-hour flight when the outside Static Air Temperature (SAT) is -56°C?
options: High-wattage electric immersion heater coils inside every wing rib bay
Aerodynamic friction heating ('Ram Rise' / Total Air Temperature) on the wing skin plus heat transfer through the engine Fuel-Cooled Oil Cooler (FCOC)
Mixing 30% automotive antifreeze into the fuel truck before departure
Pressurizing the wing tanks to 3,000 psi
explanation: At Mach 0.82, air friction and compression warm the wing skin (Total Air Temperature) by ~25°C above SAT, and before fuel enters the engine filter, hot engine oil warms it inside the Fuel-Cooled Oil Cooler (FCOC).

question: How does a modern aircraft Fuel Quantity Indicating System (FQIS) accurately measure fuel mass in kilograms despite fuel expanding and contracting with temperature?
options: Using simple mechanical cork floats connected to potentiometers
Using tubular capacitance probes (whose dielectric constant varies with fuel level and density) combined with densitometers/compensators
Using ultrasonic cameras mounted on the upper wing skin
By counting rotations of the refueling truck meter only
explanation: Capacitive fuel probes use Jet A-1 as the dielectric between two concentric metal tubes. Because the dielectric constant of kerosene varies with density, capacitance probes (with compensators/densitometers) measure true fuel mass rather than just volume.

question: What is the purpose of the Nitrogen Generation System (NGS / OBIGGS) in ATA 28 / 47 on modern airliners?
options: To re-inflate landing gear tyres automatically during flight
To pump nitrogen-enriched air into the Center Wing Tank ullage space so oxygen stays below 12% and fuel vapours cannot ignite
To supply emergency breathing gas to the passenger cabin masks
To cool the cockpit avionics racks during ground turnarounds
explanation: Developed after the 1996 TWA Flight 800 investigation, the NGS uses Air Separation Modules (ASMs) to separate oxygen from bleed air and flood the fuel tank air space with inert nitrogen-enriched air (<12% O2).
source: FAA SFAR 88 / ATA 47 Inert Gas System

question: How is emergency oxygen generated for passengers when the yellow masks drop in most commercial airliners (like the A320 and B737)?
options: From a single massive 3,000 psi liquid oxygen tank in the tailcone
By pulling the mask lanyard, which triggers a firing pin on an overhead Chemical Oxygen Generator containing Sodium Chlorate and Iron powder
By diverting compressed bleed air straight from the engines into the masks
By electrolysis of potable water from the galley tanks
explanation: Pulling a passenger mask pulls a retaining pin from a percussion cap, igniting iron powder and thermally decomposing a solid brick of Sodium Chlorate (NaClO3) into harmless salt (NaCl) and breathable oxygen gas for 12–22 minutes.

question: Why does the flight deck (cockpit crew) oxygen system use high-pressure gaseous oxygen cylinders with Quick-Donning masks rather than chemical oxygen generators?
options: Chemical oxygen generators are too heavy to mount in the cockpit ceiling
Crew masks must provide 100% pure oxygen under positive pressure to keep toxic smoke and fumes out of the pilots' lungs and goggles during an in-flight fire
Pilots require oxygen continuously from takeoff to landing on every flight
Gaseous cylinders never require hydrostatic testing or pressure checks
explanation: Passenger masks mix cabin air with oxygen (which would inhale smoke during a fire). Flight crew quick-donning masks seal tightly and can supply 100% oxygen under positive pressure to prevent smoke ingress.

question: Why is Cockpit Window Heat turned ON before every flight, even on a warm +30°C sunny afternoon?
options: To burn off insects that hit the glass during takeoff
To keep the thick inner vinyl (PVB) interlayer warm and elastic so it can stretch like a net and survive a high-speed bird strike without shattering
To improve VHF radio reception through the cockpit windows
To prevent the windshield wipers from sticking to the glass
explanation: At freezing altitude temperatures, the Polyvinyl Butyral (PVB) plastic interlayer inside laminated cockpit windshields becomes brittle. Heating it to ~40°C keeps the vinyl resilient so it absorbs bird-strike impact energy.

question: How are the wing leading-edge slats and engine air intakes anti-iced on an Airbus A320 or Boeing 737?
options: By inflating and deflating black rubber pneumatic boots on the leading edge
By routing hot pneumatic bleed air tapped from the engine compressor through internal piccolo tubes inside the leading edges
By spraying green Type IV de-icing gel from nozzles on the nosecone in flight
By circulating hot purple Skydrol hydraulic fluid through the wingtips
explanation: Jet transport aircraft route hot engine compressor bleed air through perforated 'piccolo' ducts along the inside of the engine cowl lip and outboard wing leading-edge slats to prevent ice accretion.

question: When an Engine Fire Handle (or ENG FIRE pushbutton) is pulled in the cockpit, what happens immediately?
options: Both Halon fire bottles automatically discharge into the engine core intake
Fuel LP valve, hydraulic fire shutoff valve, bleed air valve, and generator are all isolated, and the fire bottle squibs are armed
The thrust reverser deploys to slow the aircraft down
The engine starter motor engages automatically to blow the fire out
explanation: Pulling the Engine Fire switch isolates all flammable fluids, electricity, and cabin bleed air from that engine and arms the explosive discharge squibs—requiring a second deliberate action (twisting/pressing Agent 1) to fire the Halon bottle.

question: How do modern Class C belly cargo hold fire suppression systems keep a luggage fire under control during a 180-minute ETOPS ocean diversion?
options: By opening belly doors to vent all air into the stratosphere
By spraying 2,000 litres of potable water from overhead sprinkler nozzles
By sealing off cargo ventilation valves, firing a High-Rate Halon bottle for initial knockdown, and slowly metering a second Low-Rate Halon bottle over hours
By flooding the cargo hold with engine exhaust gas
explanation: Class C cargo compartments isolate ventilation to starve oxygen, discharge a high-rate Halon 1301 shot to knock down flames, and then trickle Halon through a metering system to maintain a >3% inert concentration until landing.

question: Why are lavatory sink and galley 'grey water' drain masts on the bottom of the fuselage electrically heated?
options: To boil away bacteria before the water touches the runway
To prevent grey water vented overboard in flight from freezing into heavy blocks of ice at -56°C that could strike the tail or engines
To keep the cabin floor warm near the galley doors
To generate steam for the cabin humidifiers
explanation: Sink and galley grey water is drained continuously overboard via aerodynamic drain masts; electric heaters prevent the water from freezing solid on the mast tip at high altitude.

question: Above approximately 16,000 feet in cruise, what provides the suction to flush an aircraft vacuum toilet?
options: A high-pressure hydraulic motor mounted under each toilet seat
The natural pressure differential (~8.5 psi) between the pressurized cabin and the aft waste tank (which is vented to the low-pressure outside atmosphere)
Bleed air tapped directly off the #2 engine fan
Gravity alone
explanation: On the ground and at low altitude, an electric Vacuum Blower creates suction in the waste tank. Above ~16,000 feet, the ambient outside pressure is so much lower than cabin pressure that natural differential pressure flushes the line without running the blower.

question: What is the purpose of the tiny 1.5 mm 'Bleed Hole' (breather hole) near the bottom of a passenger cabin window?
options: To allow fresh outside air to trickle directly into the passenger cabin

To equalize cabin air pressure between the inner and outer window panes so that the thick outer pane carries 100% of normal pressurization load while the middle pane stays unloaded as a fail-safe backup
To drain rainwater that leaks past the outside window frame
To allow mechanics to inject cleaning fluid between the panes
explanation: The bleed hole in the middle acrylic pane equalizes pressure across the middle pane so the outer structural pane takes the normal pressure load, leaving the middle pane unstressed as a reserve backup and preventing inter-pane condensation.

question: What happens mechanically when a flight attendant moves a cabin door lever from DISARMED to ARMED before pushback?
options: It locks the exterior door handle so ground rescuers cannot open it from outside
It mechanically engages the evacuation slide's Girt Bar into brackets on the cabin floor threshold so opening the door pulls and inflates the slide
It pressurizes the rubber door seal with 3,000 psi hydraulic fluid
It switches on the cockpit door magnetic deadbolt
explanation: Arming the door drops the steel Girt Bar into floor brackets; if the door is opened while armed, the floor holds the girt bar and pulls the slide pack out of the door bustle, triggering pneumatic inflation. (Opening the door from the outside automatically disarms it!)

question: Why is it physically impossible for a person to open a plug-type passenger cabin door at 36,000 feet cruise altitude?
options: Because an electronic GPS lock disables the door handle above 10,000 feet
Because ~8.5 psi of cabin differential pressure exerts roughly 10 metric tonnes of outward force wedging the larger plug door against the inner fuselage frame
Because the outside -56°C cold freezes the rubber door seal solid
Because the cockpit crew holds a deadbolt switch down during cruise
explanation: At 8.5 psi differential pressure, more than 1,200 lbs of force presses outward on every square foot of the door. Because plug and semi-plug doors must move inward or lift off load-bearing stops first, no human can overcome the ~10-tonne pressure load.

question: How do modern carbon-fiber composite aircraft (such as the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350) safely conduct a 200,000-amp lightning strike across the exterior skin without burning the epoxy resin?
options: They use thick rubber tyres that block lightning from hitting the aircraft in the air
They laminate a fine woven layer of expanded copper or bronze foil mesh into the outer ply of the carbon-fiber skin to act as a metallic Faraday cage
They spray conductive silver paint over the cabin windows
Carbon fiber naturally conducts electricity 10 times better than aluminum
explanation: Because carbon-fiber composite is roughly 1,000 times more resistive than aluminum, manufacturers embed an ultra-thin expanded copper or bronze mesh in the outer skin layer to dissipate lightning current safely across the surface.

question: What is the true function of the small rod-like 'Static Dischargers' (static wicks) mounted along the trailing edges of wings, ailerons, and stabilizers?
options: To attract and catch lightning bolts during thunderstorms
To bleed continuous triboelectric friction static smoothly into the slipstream so it doesn't arc across control hinges and cause VHF radio noise
To measure wake turbulence behind the wingtips
To dump excess fuel vapour out of the wing surge tanks
explanation: Air, dust, and ice crystals rubbing against the airframe build up high-voltage static charges. Static wicks provide a low-resistance corona-discharge point to bleed that static smoothly into the wake without radio interference.
source: ATA 23 / ATA 51 Bonding and Static Dischargers

question: On a high-bypass turbofan engine, what do the cockpit gauges 'N1' and 'N2' represent?
options: N1 is oil pressure and N2 is fuel flow
N1 is the rotational speed (% RPM) of the Low-Pressure Fan/Compressor spool, and N2 is the rotational speed (% RPM) of the High-Pressure core spool
N1 is Engine #1 speed and N2 is Engine #2 speed
N1 is forward thrust and N2 is reverse thrust
explanation: In a twin-spool turbofan, N1 measures the Low-Pressure (LP) shaft RPM (the big front fan and LP compressor driven by the LP turbine), while N2 measures the High-Pressure (HP) core shaft RPM (which drives the accessory gearbox).

question: What does declining 'EGT Margin' (Exhaust Gas Temperature Margin) on a jet engine indicate to CAMO powerplant engineers?
options: The engine is running cooler and more efficiently than when it was new
Compressor and turbine blade tip clearances and airfoils are wearing/fouling, forcing the engine to burn more fuel and run closer to its certified Redline EGT limit to produce takeoff thrust
The aircraft's fuel tanks are contaminated with water
The engine oil cooler is over-cooling the oil during cruise
explanation: EGT Margin is the temperature headroom between peak takeoff EGT and the certified Redline limit. As internal blade clearances widen with age, compressor efficiency drops, requiring higher fuel flow and higher EGT to hit target thrust.

question: During a jet engine start sequence, what is a 'Hot Start'?
options: Starting the engine on a sunny afternoon when ramp temperature is above 35°C
An abnormal start where Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) exceeds the certified starting limit because fuel was introduced with insufficient airflow/N2 rotation
Using the APU to start both engines at the exact same time
Pre-heating the engine oil with an electric blanket before flight
explanation: A Hot Start occurs when fuel ignites in the combustor without enough compressor airflow (low starter pressure, tailwind in tailpipe, or excessive fuel scheduling) to cool the turbine, causing EGT to spike toward or past redline.

question: How does a jet engine Thrust Reverser slow the aircraft down after landing?
options: By stopping the turbine shaft and spinning the front fan blades in the opposite direction
By deploying blocker doors/cascades that deflect cold fan bypass air (or exhaust) forward and outward at roughly a 45-degree angle
By locking the engine accessory gearbox with a carbon disc brake
By opening a drag parachute out of the engine tailcone
explanation: Jet engines never spin backward. Instead, hydraulic or pneumatic actuators slide the outer translating cowl rearward, swinging blocker doors into the bypass duct to redirect fan air forward through cascade vanes.

question: Why are transport aircraft certified with a 'Limit Load' of +2.5G and an 'Ultimate Load' of +3.75G (a 1.5x safety factor)?
options: So commercial airliners can perform aerobatic loops during test flights
So the airframe can withstand the maximum aerodynamic load expected in service (+2.5G) with zero permanent deformation, and hold 150% of that load (+3.75G) for 3 seconds without structural failure
Because cabin seats weigh 1.5 times more when passengers recline them
To allow the aircraft to land at 1.5 times its Maximum Takeoff Weight
explanation: Under CS-25 / FAR 25.303, Limit Load is the maximum load expected in service (no permanent set/yield allowed), while Ultimate Load (1.5 × Limit Load) is the point below which the structure must not fracture.
source: EASA CS-25 / FAR Part 25 Structural Loads

question: What is 'Damage-Tolerant Design' in modern aircraft structures?
options: Building the skin out of solid armor plate so it can never dent
Engineering multiple parallel load paths and tear straps so that if a fatigue crack or damage occurs, the remaining structure safely carries flight loads until scheduled inspections detect the crack
Allowing an aircraft to fly indefinitely without ever inspecting for cracks
Making wings rigid so they never flex in turbulence
explanation: Damage tolerance assumes microscopic flaws or service damage can occur, using fail-safe multi-load-path structures and fracture-mechanics inspection intervals to guarantee any crack is caught long before reaching critical length.

question: In aircraft structural blueprints and Dent & Buckle charts, what do 'Fuselage Station (STA)', 'Waterline (WL)', and 'Buttock Line (BL) / Stringer (STR)' measure?
options: Airspeed, altitude, and rate of climb
Longitudinal distance from nose datum (STA), vertical height (WL), and lateral/circumferential distance from centerline (BL/STR)
Fuel tank capacity, water tank level, and waste tank weight
Paint thickness, rivet diameter, and bolt torque
explanation: Aircraft 3D structural coordinates locate any rivet or dent precisely using Station/Frame (fore-to-aft X-axis), Waterline (vertical Z-axis), and Buttock Line or Stringer number (lateral/circumferential Y-axis).
source: ATA 06 / ATA 53 Structural Dimensions and Areas

question: Why must an aircraft's Pitot Probes, Static Ports, and Angle-of-Attack (AoA) vanes be protected with bright red covers whenever the aircraft is parked for storage?
options: To stop ultraviolet sunlight from fading the silver metal
To prevent insects (like mud-dauber wasps), dust, sand, or water from entering the tiny pressure tubes and causing fatal airspeed/altimeter errors on takeoff
To keep the cockpit warm overnight
To prevent mechanics from accidentally painting the cockpit windows
explanation: Blocked pitot or static ports corrupt Indicated Airspeed and altitude readings in flight (a known cause of fatal accidents such as Birgenair 301 and Aeroperú 603). Pitot/static covers prevent insect nests and FOD ingress on the ground.

question: What is the critical difference between 'Indicated Airspeed' (IAS) measured by the Pitot-Static system and 'Ground Speed' (GS) measured by GPS?
options: There is no difference; they are always identical in cruise
IAS measures the actual dynamic pressure of air molecules flowing over the wing (which governs stall and structural overspeed limits), whereas GS only measures speed over the Earth's surface
GPS Ground Speed is used to calculate wing stall speed in clouds
Indicated Airspeed only works below 10,000 feet
explanation: An aircraft wing only cares about the dynamic pressure of the air molecules striking it (Indicated Airspeed). At 38,000 feet in thin air with a tailwind, Ground Speed may be 550 knots while IAS is only 250 knots.

question: When TCAS II (Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System) issues a red 'Resolution Advisory' (RA) like 'CLIMB, CLIMB!', which direction of maneuver can TCAS II command?
options: Sharp left or right 45-degree bank turns only
Vertical pitch maneuvers ONLY (Climb, Descend, Level Off, or Maintain Vertical Speed)—never horizontal turns
Automatic deployment of speedbrakes and landing gear
Switching off the engines to reduce speed
explanation: At 500 knots, horizontal turn radii are too wide and slow to resolve an imminent collision in 25 seconds. TCAS II resolves conflicts exclusively in the vertical plane, coordinating between both aircraft via Mode S data link.

question: What happens if a TCAS Resolution Advisory (RA) commands 'CLIMB!' at the exact same moment Air Traffic Control on the radio orders 'DESCEND!'?
options: The pilot must always obey the human Air Traffic Controller
The pilot must immediately follow the TCAS RA ('CLIMB!') and notify ATC afterward, because both aircrafts' TCAS computers have coordinated complementary vertical paths
The pilot must split the difference and fly level
The autopilot automatically shuts off all cockpit screens
explanation: Following the 2002 Überlingen mid-air collision, global aviation rules mandate that pilots strictly follow TCAS Resolution Advisories even if they conflict with ATC instructions.

question: Why are the Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) and Flight Data Recorder (FDR) painted bright International Orange and mounted in the rear tailcone?
options: Because the tailcone has better Wi-Fi signal for passengers
Orange maximizes visual recovery in wreckage, and the forward fuselage/wings act as a crumple zone so the rear tailcone experiences the lowest deceleration G-forces in a crash
To balance the weight of the nose radar dish
Because the tailcone is pressurized to twice normal cabin pressure
explanation: Mounting flight recorders in the aft unpressurized tailcone places them farthest from initial impact forces and main wing fuel tanks, while high-visibility International Orange aids search teams.

question: Under the Minimum Equipment List (MEL), what is the standard maximum rectification interval for a 'Category C' deferred defect?
options: 3 consecutive calendar days (72 hours), excluding the day of discovery
10 consecutive calendar days (240 hours), excluding the day of discovery
120 consecutive calendar days, excluding the day of discovery
Before the next flight departure
explanation: MEL repair intervals (starting at 00:01 UTC the day after discovery) are: Category A (custom interval stated in remarks), Category B (3 calendar days), Category C (10 calendar days), and Category D (120 calendar days).
source: EASA Part-M / DGCA CAR-M MEL Rules

question: In an Airline's Minimum Equipment List (MEL), what do the symbols '(M)' and '(O)' next to an item indicate?
options: Mandatory replacement and Optional replacement
Mechanical system and Oxygen system
A mandatory Maintenance procedure (M) required to lock out/deactivate the item, and an Operational procedure (O) for the flight crew before dispatch
Main base repair only and Outstation repair allowed
explanation: (M) indicates a specific Maintenance deactivation/securing procedure that normally must be carried out and certified by a licensed engineer prior to flight, while (O) indicates a special flight crew Operational procedure.

question: What is the key difference between a Minimum Equipment List (MEL) and a Configuration Deviation List (CDL)?
options: The MEL is for Boeing aircraft and the CDL is for Airbus aircraft

The MEL covers inoperative internal systems/instruments still installed on the aircraft, whereas the CDL covers external secondary structural/aerodynamic parts (like fairings or seals) that are physically missing
The CDL only applies during heavy C-Checks inside a hangar
The MEL is approved by the manufacturer while the CDL requires no approval
explanation: The MEL governs dispatch with inoperative systems/equipment, whereas the CDL (part of the Aircraft Flight Manual) governs dispatch when external secondary structural panels, seals, or static wicks are missing—often with a takeoff weight penalty.

question: Why are some manufacturer Service Bulletins (SBs) legally optional for a commercial airline, whereas Airworthiness Directives (ADs) are strictly mandatory?
options: Service Bulletins only apply to cabin paint colors

Manufacturers (Airbus, Boeing, CFM) are private companies that recommend reliability or product improvements via SBs, whereas only a statutory Aviation Authority (EASA, FAA, DGCA) can mandate law via an AD
Airworthiness Directives are written by airline pilots
Service Bulletins automatically expire after 30 days
explanation: An OEM Service Bulletin is legally non-mandatory unless it is mandated by a National Aviation Authority through an Airworthiness Directive (AD) or required contractually by an aircraft lease agreement.

question: Under EASA and DGCA regulations, what are the two conditions required for an aircraft to be considered legally 'Airworthy'?
options: It has full fuel tanks and two qualified pilots onboard
It conforms strictly to its approved Type Certificate design (including approved modifications/repairs) AND is in a condition for safe operation
It is less than 25 years old and painted white
It has passed a daily walkaround inspection by the ramp agent
explanation: The legal test for airworthiness has two halves: 1) Conformity to the approved Type Certificate (every part, mod, and AD properly documented), and 2) Condition for safe operation (no wear or defects beyond AMM/MEL limits).

question: What is the relationship between an aircraft's Certificate of Airworthiness (C of A) and its Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC)?
options: They are two names for the exact same document
The C of A is non-expiring, but it remains legally valid ONLY when accompanied by a current, in-date Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC) renewed/extended every 12 months
The ARC is issued only once at the factory, while the C of A expires every 30 days
An ARC is only required for cargo freighter aircraft
explanation: Under EASA Part-M / Part-CAMO and DGCA CAR-M, the C of A does not carry an expiration date, but its validity depends on having a valid 1-year Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC).

question: If an aircraft remains continuously in a 'Controlled Environment' (managed by the same approved CAMO with no operator changes), how many times can its Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC) be extended before a full new physical and records review is required?
options: Never; a full physical survey is required every 6 months
Twice (for 12 months each time), creating a 3-year cycle between full Airworthiness Reviews
Ten times (once per year for 10 years)
Indefinitely until the aircraft is retired
explanation: In a Controlled Environment, an approved CAMO can issue an ARC in Year 1, extend it in Year 2, and extend it a second time in Year 3—after which a full documentary and physical Airworthiness Review must be performed.

question: Why does aviation regulation separate the Continuing Airworthiness Management Organisation (CAMO) from the Approved Maintenance Organisation (Part-145 / CAR-145)?
options: So mechanics don't have to use computers
To separate the 'Brain' that plans maintenance, tracks ADs/LLPs, and audits records (CAMO) from the 'Hands' that execute the physical wrench work and sign the CRS (Part-145)
Because Part-145 organizations are only allowed to paint aircraft
Because CAMOs only manage retired aircraft stored in deserts
explanation: Separating planning/records control (CAMO) from maintenance execution (Part-145) ensures an independent quality loop and keeps total airworthiness control under one roof even when an airline outsources hangar checks globally.
source: EASA Part-CAMO & Part-145 / DGCA CAR-M & CAR-145

question: When a third-party company (other than the original aircraft manufacturer) designs a major modification—such as installing a satellite Wi-Fi radome or converting a passenger jet into a freighter—what regulatory approval is issued?
options: A Minimum Equipment List (MEL)
A Supplemental Type Certificate (STC)
An Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC)
A Certificate of Release to Service (CRS)
explanation: Only the original manufacturer holds the Type Certificate (TC). When any other approved Design Organisation (Part-21J) obtains design approval for a major modification, the authority issues a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC).
source: EASA Part-21 Subpart E / FAA Part 21

question: How can an aircraft with un-repaired fuselage damage beyond SRM/MEL limits legally fly from a small outstation airport to a major maintenance hangar for repair?
options: By turning off its transponder and flying at night
Under a one-time 'Permit to Fly' (Special Flight Permit / Ferry Permit) with approved Flight Conditions, zero passengers onboard, and strict speed/altitude/pressurization restrictions
By writing 'Category D MEL' in the cabin logbook and boarding passengers normally
It can never fly again and must be disassembled at the outstation
explanation: When an aircraft's normal C of A is temporarily invalid due to damage or an overdue check, the authority/CAMO (with OEM engineering Flight Conditions) can issue a one-time Permit to Fly (Ferry Permit) with essential crew only.
source: EASA Part-21 Subpart P / DGCA CAR

question: In ETOPS (Extended Diversion Time Operations) line maintenance, why is the same mechanic normally prohibited from changing oil filters or magnetic chip detectors on BOTH engines during the same turnaround?
options: Because changing two oil filters takes more than 8 hours
To prevent a 'Common-Mode Human Maintenance Error' (like forgetting an O-ring seal on both engines) that could cause both engines to fail simultaneously over an ocean
Because Engine #1 and Engine #2 use completely different brands of oil
Because ETOPS aircraft only have one engine
explanation: Dual Maintenance Prohibition prevents a single human error from compromising both powerplants on the same flight—requiring separate maintenance crews, staggered flights, or a verification test between tasks.

question: Why are commercial aircraft registrations in India prefixed with 'VT-' (e.g., VT-ANL) while Irish leased aircraft often use 'EI-'?
options: VT stands for 'Vertical Takeoff' and EI stands for 'Engine Installed'
Aircraft registration prefixes are sovereign ICAO Nationality Marks ('VT' allocated to India in 1929; 'EI' allocated to Ireland), indicating which State of Registry's laws govern the aircraft
The prefix indicates the manufacturer of the engines
Airlines can pick any two random letters they like for each flight
explanation: Under ICAO Annex 7, the prefix denotes the sovereign State of Registry (VT- for India under the DGCA, EI- for Ireland, N- for the USA, G- for the UK), which holds legal airworthiness oversight of that tail number.
source: ICAO Annex 7 Aircraft Nationality and Registration Marks

question: What does 'CDCCL' (Critical Design Configuration Control Limitations) mean when highlighted inside an Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) fuel-tank task?
options: A suggestion that mechanics can skip if they are short on time
A mandatory fuel-tank ignition-prevention design feature (such as specific wire separation gaps or bonding resistance limits) that must NEVER be altered during maintenance
A chart showing how much fuel to load for short-haul flights
A list of cabin cleaning detergents
explanation: Created after the TWA 800 fuel tank explosion (SFAR 88 / Fuel Tank Safety), a CDCCL locks critical design features (wire routing separation, bonding jumper resistance, spark barriers) so maintenance never introduces an ignition source.
source: EASA Fuel Tank Safety / FAA SFAR 88

question: Why did aviation regulators elevate 'EWIS' (Electrical Wiring Interconnect System) into its own dedicated airworthiness discipline?
options: To make aircraft wiring heavier and thicker
Because aging, chafed, or contaminated wire bundles can suffer 3,000°C 'Arc Tracking' that burns through nearby systems and insulation without tripping standard thermal circuit breakers
To replace all copper wires with wireless Bluetooth transmitters
Because cockpit pilots have to re-wire the instrument panel before every flight
explanation: Following accidents like Swissair Flight 111, regulators recognized that wiring is an aging system subject to chafing, wet arc tracking, and lint contamination—mandating EZAP zonal inspections, drip loops, and strict clamping rules.

question: Why must every new batch of aircraft seat cushion covers, carpets, or curtains be accompanied by a laboratory 'Flammability / Burn Test Certificate' (CS/FAR 25.853)?
options: To prove the fabric color won't fade when washed
To verify the cabin materials are self-extinguishing and resist 'Flashover' and toxic smoke release, preserving the 90-second passenger evacuation window
To make sure the seats are soft enough for long-haul flights
To calculate the aircraft's Center of Gravity
explanation: Under CS/FAR 25.853, cabin materials must pass vertical Bunsen burner and/or 1,038°C kerosene oil-burner fire-blocking tests. Missing burn certificates during a lease return or ARC audit render the cabin non-compliant.

question: In aviation technical records, what does the term 'Dirty Fingerprints' (DFP) refer to?
options: Grease smudges left on passenger cabin windows by mechanics
The original physical or scanned task cards, work orders, and release certificates signed and stamped by the certifying engineer at the time maintenance or an AD/SB was accomplished
Forensic police evidence collected after a security incident
An unwashed engine compressor blade
explanation: A summary printout from AMOS or Excel is not legal proof of AD/SB compliance. Auditors require the 'Dirty Fingerprints' (DFP)—the actual signed, stamped task card and certified work package from the hangar floor.
source: IATA / IALTA Technical Records Best Practices

question: Why does a single missing document in the 'Back-to-Birth' (BtB) traceability chain of an engine Life-Limited Part (LLP) reduce that $350,000 titanium disc to scrap value?
options: Because the disc won't physically fit inside the engine without the paper
Because sub-microscopic low-cycle fatigue cannot be measured by NDT X-rays—if total accumulated Flight Cycles since factory manufacture cannot be proven without gaps, the part is legally unairworthy
Because the airline gets fined $1 million by the airport authority
Because LLPs must be replaced after every single flight
explanation: LLPs (rotating engine discs/spools whose failure would be uncontained) have a strict safe-life cycle limit. Since NDT cannot measure pre-crack atomic fatigue, any gap in Back-to-Birth cycle history makes it impossible to verify remaining life.

question: Why are commercial aircraft tracked by THREE separate clocks simultaneously: Flight Hours (FH), Flight Cycles (FC), and Calendar Time?
options: Because pilots in different time zones use different watches
Because continuous-run parts wear by Hours (FH), pressurized hulls/landing gear/engine discs fatigue by takeoffs & landings (FC), and corrosion/seals/slides age by Calendar Days/Months
To make maintenance spreadsheets three times longer
Because FAA tracks hours, EASA tracks cycles, and DGCA tracks calendar days
explanation: Different physical degradation mechanisms govern different parts: continuous friction/erosion scales with Flight Hours (FH), cyclic pressurization and thermal shock scale with Flight Cycles (FC), and corrosion/chemical aging scale with Calendar Time.

question: On an Authorised Release Certificate (EASA Form 1, FAA Form 8130-3, or DGCA CA Form 1), what is the difference between signing the LEFT side (Block 13) vs. the RIGHT side (Block 14)?
options: Left side is for Airbus parts; Right side is for Boeing parts

Left side (Block 13) is signed by an Approved Manufacturer (Part-21G) for a BRAND-NEW part; Right side (Block 14) is signed by an Approved Maintenance/Repair Station (Part-145) for a USED/REPAIRED/OVERHAULED part
Left side is signed by the mechanic; Right side is signed by the pilot
There is no difference; either side can be signed for any part
explanation: An Authorised Release Certificate serves two distinct legal regimes: Block 13 (Left) certifies conformity of a newly manufactured part under Part-21, whereas Block 14 (Right) is the Certificate of Release to Service (CRS) for a maintained/overhauled part under Part-145.
source: EASA Appendix II to Part-M (EASA Form 1 Instructions)

question: Why do global aircraft lessors strictly require a 'Dual Release' (EASA Part-145 + FAA Part 145) on overhauled components installed during a lease?
options: So the repair shop can charge twice as much money
So the component is legally accepted under both EASA and FAA jurisdictions, allowing the lessor to transition the aircraft seamlessly to any airline worldwide at lease end
Because two mechanics must carry heavy parts together
Dual Release is only required for passenger cabin seats
explanation: A single-release FAA 8130-3 is not accepted on an EASA-registered aircraft (and vice versa). Requiring Dual Release guarantees global asset portability across EASA, FAA, and DGCA registries without re-overhauling parts.
source: US-EU Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreement (BASA) / Lease Return Conditions

question: What document serves as the legal factory 'Birth Certificate' of a brand-new Airbus aircraft leaving the assembly line under EASA Part-21G?
options: The Minimum Equipment List (MEL)
The EASA Form 52 (Aircraft Statement of Conformity) or initial Export C of A, accompanied by the Aircraft Inspection Report (AIR)
A fuel receipt from Toulouse airport
The captain's pilot license
explanation: The manufacturer issues an EASA Form 52 (or initial Export C of A) and the factory Aircraft Inspection Report (AIR) / Delivery Readiness Log (DRL), which establishes Day-1 conformity and acts as the birth record for all original factory-installed parts.

question: Why must an airline issue a signed 'Non-Incident / Non-Accident Statement' (NIS) whenever an engine, LLP, landing gear, or aircraft finishes a lease or enters an overhaul shop?
options: To congratulate the pilots on good landings
Because extreme crash loads, fire heat, or saltwater submersion cause invisible metallurgical damage (like loss of heat-treatment temper) that normal NDT inspections cannot reliably detect
To calculate airport landing fees
To renew the cabin crew's uniforms
explanation: High-strength alloys subjected to extreme fire heat or crash shock can lose their metallurgical temper without visible cracks. An unbroken chain of Operator NIS letters certifies the part was never exposed to disqualifying trauma or military service.
source: IATA / AWG Aircraft Leasing Technical Standards

question: What are the three component maintenance philosophies defined under MSG-3: 'HT', 'OC', and 'CM'?
options: High Temperature, Over Cooled, and Cabin Mounted
Hard-Time (fixed overhaul/scrap limit), On-Condition (periodic wear inspection/test), and Condition-Monitored (non-critical/redundant items allowed to operate to failure with reliability tracking)
Heavy Tooling, Optical Check, and Calibrated Meter
Hangar Test, Outstation Check, and Cockpit Monitor
explanation: Hard-Time (HT) parts have a mandatory removal limit (FH/FC/Calendar); On-Condition (OC) parts remain installed as long as they pass periodic wear checks; Condition-Monitored (CM) redundant parts fly until failure while CAMO tracks fleet reliability.

question: Why are commercial aircraft engines frequently owned and leased separately from the airframe they are bolted onto?
options: Because engines are made of titanium and airframes are made of aluminum
Because two engines represent ~50% of an aircraft's value and require 60–120 day off-wing shop visits—requiring airlines to swap spare/leased pool engines onto the wing so the airframe keeps flying
Because aviation law forbids an airline from owning both a wing and an engine
Because engines never require maintenance records
explanation: Engines are high-value rotable assets tracked independently by Engine Serial Number (ESN) under the Cape Town Convention. When an engine goes into a 90-day shop visit, a spare or short-term leased engine takes its place overnight.

question: What happens during a 'Maintenance Programme Bridging Check' when a used aircraft transitions from Airline A to Airline B?
options: The aircraft is flown underneath a suspension bridge to test its altimeters
CAMO engineers compare every MPD/AMP task interval between the outgoing and incoming operators and perform any tasks that are due or overdue under the new airline's approved schedule
The wings are unbolted and swapped with another aircraft
All historical maintenance records are shredded to start fresh at zero hours
explanation: Different airlines have different approved task intervals based on environment and utilization. Bridging aligns the aircraft's maintenance clock from the previous operator's AMP to the incoming operator's AMP before its first revenue flight.

question: In aircraft leasing, why do airlines pay monthly 'Maintenance Reserves' (Supplemental Rent) based on Flight Hours and Flight Cycles flown?
options: To pay for the pilots' hotel rooms at outstations

To accumulate cash in ring-fenced pots matching the mechanical life burned each month on Engines, LLPs, Landing Gear, APU, and Heavy Checks—protecting the lessor if the airline defaults before overhaul
To pay airport air traffic control navigation charges
As a non-refundable tip to the aircraft manufacturer
explanation: As an aircraft flies, it consumes millions of dollars of built-in maintenance life. Monthly Maintenance Reserves ensure cash is set aside per hour/cycle flown, which the airline claims back when a qualifying major overhaul is completed.
source: IATA / IALTA Aircraft Leasing & Maintenance Reserves

question: What does 'ACMI' stand for in a short-term aircraft 'Wet Lease' agreement?
options: Air Conditioning, Cabin, Motors, and Instruments
Aircraft, Crew, Maintenance, and Insurance
Airbus, CFM, Michelin, and Inmarsat
Approved Certificate of Maintenance Inspection
explanation: In a Wet Lease (ACMI), the lessor provides the ready-to-fly Aircraft, Flight/Cabin Crew, Maintenance (CAMO/Part-145), and Hull Insurance for a block-hour fee, while the customer airline covers fuel, catering, and airport fees.

question: Under the international Cape Town Convention, what does an 'IDERA' (Irrevocable De-Registration and Export Request Authorisation) allow an aircraft lessor to do?
options: Fly the aircraft without pilots using remote control
Compel the national aviation authority (such as the DGCA) to deregister and permit export of a leased aircraft within days if the airline defaults on lease payments
Change the aircraft's engine thrust rating without OEM permission
Exempt the aircraft from all Airworthiness Directives
explanation: Signed by the airline at lease inception and filed with the aviation authority, an IDERA grants the lessor the pre-authorized legal right to deregister and export their aircraft swiftly upon lease default.
source: Cape Town Convention / DGCA IDERA Rules

question: Why must transport aircraft Landing Gear legs undergo a complete off-wing Hard-Time overhaul every 10 to 12 calendar years regardless of how few hours the aircraft has flown?
options: Because rubber tyres expire after 10 years

Because ultra-high-strength steel (300M) forgings are susceptible to calendar-driven Stress-Corrosion Cracking under bushings and chrome plating, requiring complete chemical stripping, NDT, re-plating, and baking
Because landing gear paint changes color every decade
Because the cockpit gear lever wears out after 10 years
explanation: Moisture and static weight loads drive time-dependent stress-corrosion in high-strength steel hidden beneath pressed bushings and hard chrome plating—requiring full disassembly, chemical stripping, NDT, re-plating, and hydrogen de-embrittlement baking.

question: Why do only ~1,800 out of nearly 3,000 tasks in the Airbus A320 Maintenance Planning Document (MPD) actually apply to any single aircraft tail number?
options: Airlines are allowed to randomly delete 1,200 tasks to save money
Each MPD task has an 'Effectivity / Applicability' rule filtered by the specific aircraft's Engine type, Weight Variant, and Pre-Mod / Post-Mod (Service Bulletin) configuration status
The other 1,200 tasks only apply to helicopters
Only the first 1,800 pages of the manual are printed
explanation: Across decades of production, design Modifications (Mods) and Service Bulletins (SBs) change components and structures. CAMO engineers evaluate each MPD task's Effectivity expression against the specific MSN's Mod/SB status.
source: Airbus MPD General Introduction / CAMO Planning

question: What happens when structural damage on an airframe exceeds the allowable repair limits published in the Structural Repair Manual (SRM)?
options: The mechanic puts three layers of Speed Tape over the crack and signs the logbook
CAMO engineering must request a custom 'Repair Design Approval' (Major/Minor Repair Disposition) from the OEM (Airbus/Boeing) or an approved Part-21J / DER design organization
The pilot flies the aircraft unpressurized forever
The damage is ignored until the next 12-year D-Check
explanation: The SRM only covers pre-approved standard repairs. Any damage outside SRM boundaries requires custom stress-engineered drawings approved by the Type Certificate Holder (OEM) or a Part-21J / DER authority.

question: In aircraft valuation and lease return conditions, what does 'Half-Life Condition' mean?
options: The aircraft is 15 years old out of a 30-year lifespan
Every major time-controlled asset (Engines, LLPs, Landing Gear, APU, and Heavy Checks) is at exactly 50% of its overhaul interval or remaining life
Half of the passenger cabin seats have been removed
The aircraft is only allowed to fly with half-full fuel tanks
explanation: 'Half-Life' is the standard aviation appraisal benchmark where 50% of the time/cycles between overhauls (or LLP life) remains on each major cost component; deviations above or below Half-Life are adjusted financially in dollars per hour/cycle.

question: Why does an engine Life-Limited Part (LLP) require 'Pro-Rata' life calculation if the engine was operated at two different thrust ratings during its career?
options: Because different airlines use different currencies
Because running the exact same physical disc at a higher thrust rating subjects it to higher centrifugal and thermal stress—giving it a lower certified Cycle Limit than at a lower thrust rating
Because thrust ratings change the diameter of the fan blades
Pro-rata calculation is only used for cabin carpets
explanation: Changing an engine's rating plug changes its takeoff thrust and internal stress. An LLP might have a 20,000-cycle limit at low thrust and a 15,000-cycle limit at high thrust—requiring fractional pro-rata math across each historical period.

question: When an aging airliner is retired at age 25 for a 'Part-Out / Teardown', why must mechanics carefully unbolt components per the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) instead of cutting them out quickly?
options: To keep the hangar floor quiet

Because any harvested component (USM — Used Serviceable Material) can only be overhauled and issued a legal EASA Form 1 / FAA 8130-3 if it was removed per approved AMM procedures with full traceability and an NIS
Because saws are banned inside airports
So the airplane can be bolted back together the next week
explanation: A retired jet's engines, APU, landing gear, and avionics are worth millions as Used Serviceable Material (USM), but only if removed per the AMM by an approved Part-145 organization with unbroken traceability to the final component status list.
source: AFRA Best Management Practice for Aircraft Decommissioning

question: In an Engine Shop Visit (ESV) binder, why is the final 'Test Cell Run Report' one of the most important pages audited by lessors and CAMO engineers?
options: It shows how much paint was used on the engine cowling
It proves the rebuilt engine ran at full takeoff power inside a calibrated test cell and met all thrust, vibration, oil pressure, and outbound EGT Margin requirements before release
It lists the names of the truck drivers who delivered the engine
It certifies that the cabin air conditioning filters were replaced
explanation: Before an overhauled engine can be issued its master EASA Form 1 / 8130-3 release certificate, it must pass a full-power Test Cell run verifying mechanical integrity and establishing its post-overhaul EGT Margin baseline.
source: Engine Shop Manual / ESV Audit Guidelines

question: When maintenance disturbs a primary flight control or engine control system, why do regulations mandate a 'Duplicate / Independent Inspection' by two separate qualified engineers?
options: Because flight control cables are too heavy for one person to see

To defeat human confirmation bias and catch single-point-of-failure rigging errors (such as reversed control movement, wrong cable tension, or a missing cotter pin/lockwire) before closing access panels
To train junior apprentices on where the tailcone is located
Because aviation law requires every job on an aircraft to be signed by four people
explanation: Redundancy cannot save an aircraft if an elevator or aileron is mis-rigged or comes disconnected. An Independent Inspection requires two qualified people to separately verify assembly, locking, tension, full travel, and correct sense of direction.
source: EASA Part-145.A.48 / DGCA CAR-145 Critical Maintenance Tasks

question: When lockwiring (safety wiring) two standard right-hand-thread bolts together, how must the stainless-steel wire be routed?
options: Loosely with zero twists so the bolts can rotate 90 degrees freely
In 'Positive Tension'—so that any counterclockwise loosening movement of either bolt pulls the wire tighter in the clockwise (tightening) direction of the second bolt
In 'Negative Tension' so both bolts unscrew at the same time
Wrapped around the threads underneath the nut
explanation: Lockwire must always be applied in positive (tightening) tension at 6–8 twists per inch with a safely tucked pigtail, making it mechanically impossible for either fastener to rotate counterclockwise without tightening its neighbour.

question: What is the purpose of the bright orange or red 'Torque Seal' (inspection lacquer) stripe painted across a nut and bolt thread after torquing?
options: It acts as super-strong glue that holds the nut onto the bolt
It dries into a hard, brittle crust that visibly cracks and misaligns if the nut backs off or is tampered with by even a couple of degrees
It lubricates the bolt threads for easy removal next year
It insulates the bolt from lightning strikes
explanation: Torque Seal has zero mechanical holding strength; it is a brittle visual witness mark that allows an engineer with a flashlight to instantly verify that hundreds of hydraulic B-nuts and structural bolts haven't rotated since installation.

question: What happens in an approved Part-145 / CAR-145 hangar if a mechanic finishes a job and discovers one small socket bit is missing from their shadow-foam toolbox?
options: The mechanic buys a replacement socket on the way home and says nothing
The aircraft cannot be signed off (CRS is blocked) and is placed on 'Tool Lost Hold' until a thorough search (and NDT/borescope if needed) recovers the missing tool
The pilot is asked to listen for rattling noises during takeoff
Missing tools only matter if they weigh more than 1 kilogram
explanation: A loose tool left inside an airframe is lethal Foreign Object Debris (FOD) capable of jamming flight control pulleys or shorting electrical buses. Tool Control rules block aircraft release until 100% of tools are accounted for.
source: Part-145 / CAR-145 Tool Control & FOD Prevention

question: Why are mechanics forbidden from inserting a turning tool and rotating a jet engine shaft immediately after the engine shuts down while it is still hot?
options: Because the fuel nozzles will spray fuel onto the hangar floor
Because uneven rising heat inside a stopped engine temporarily warps the shaft upward ('Thermal Rotor Bow'), causing blade tips to rub hard and seize against the top casing shroud
Because the magnetic chip detectors are still energized
Because the fan blades are magnetized when hot
explanation: After shutdown, hot air rises to the top of the engine core, causing asymmetric thermal expansion ('Rotor Bow'). Mechanics must wait for the AMM cooldown window before cranking the core for a borescope inspection.

question: Which Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) method uses a small electromagnetic coil to induce swirling electrical currents in conductive aluminum skin—capable of detecting microscopic fatigue cracks around rivet holes right through the paint?
options: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT)
Eddy Current Testing (ET)
Magnetic Particle Testing (MT)
Visual Coin-Tap Testing
explanation: Eddy Current Testing (ET) induces circular electrical currents in conductive non-ferrous metals like aluminum. A surface or near-subsurface crack interrupts the current flow and shifts coil impedance—without needing to strip exterior paint.

question: Why can't 'Magnetic Particle Testing' (MT) be used to inspect an aluminum wing skin or a titanium fan blade?
options: Because aluminum and titanium melt when exposed to magnetic fields
Because Magnetic Particle Testing only works on ferromagnetic materials (like high-strength steel landing gear pins and axles) that can be strongly magnetized
Because aluminum wings are too large to fit inside a hangar
Because MT only works on carbon-fiber composites
explanation: Aluminum, titanium, and austenitic stainless steels are non-magnetic. Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) is reserved strictly for ferromagnetic iron and steel components like landing gear forgings, bolts, and shafts.

question: What is aviation 'Speed Tape' actually made of, and what is it legally used for?
options: Cloth-backed hardware duct tape used to hold broken wing spars together
Heavy-gauge malleable aluminum foil with high-strength silicone/acrylic adhesive, approved by the SRM/AMM for covering wet sealant or protecting minor peeled paint on non-structural panels
Double-sided carpet tape used to hold passenger seats to the floor
Plastic electrical tape used to insulate pitot tubes
explanation: Speed Tape is an aerospace aluminum foil tape rated for -65°C to +300°C and 600-mph airflow. It carries zero primary structural load and is strictly regulated by the SRM/AMM for temporary aerodynamic sealing and moisture protection.

question: Why must mechanics use strictly Demineralized / Deionized pure water when performing an On-Wing Engine Compressor Water Wash?
options: Because pure water is heavier and blasts dirt harder

Because dissolved minerals (calcium, sodium, chlorides) in ordinary tap water would bake onto 1,500°C turbine blades, clogging microscopic cooling holes and causing high-temperature sulfidation corrosion
Because tap water freezes at +20°C inside an engine
Because deionized water is dyed bright purple for leak detection
explanation: Spraying mineral-laden tap water into a gas turbine leaves scale deposits inside laser-drilled turbine cooling holes and introduces sodium/chlorides that cause destructive hot corrosion on nickel superalloys.

question: During winter ground de-icing, why do trucks spray heated Orange 'Type I' fluid first, followed by cold Emerald-Green 'Type IV' fluid?
options: Orange is for Boeing jets and Green is for Airbus jets

Hot watery Type I melts and blasts off existing ice/snow, while thick shear-thinning Type IV polymer gel clings to the wing to prevent new snow from sticking until it shears off at ~100 knots during takeoff
Green fluid is sprayed to wash the orange dye off the paint
Type IV fluid freezes into a protective ice shell over the wing
explanation: Type I (orange) has low viscosity and uses heat to remove existing contamination; Type IV (green) is a thick non-Newtonian gel that provides long Holdover Time (HOT) in falling snow before liquefying under aerodynamic shear during the takeoff roll.
source: ATA 12 / ICAO Manual of Aircraft Ground De-icing

question: Why is the refueling operator required to attach a metal Bonding Cable between the fuel truck and the aircraft BEFORE opening or connecting the fuel nozzle?
options: So the fuel truck cannot drive away while the hose is attached
To equalize electrical potential between the fuel truck and the airframe so static electricity cannot jump as a spark across the nozzle gap when coupling or uncoupling
To power the fuel truck's pump using the aircraft's 400 Hz generator
To measure how many litres of fuel are in the wing
explanation: Bonding brings the fuel bowser and the aircraft to the exact same electrical voltage potential before the fuel port is opened, eliminating any possibility of a static discharge arc igniting fuel vapours.

question: When an aircraft is lifted on three hydraulic tripod jacks inside a hangar, why must mechanics continuously screw down the threaded metal 'Safety Collars' on the jack rams?
options: To measure how many inches the aircraft has been lifted
To provide a solid mechanical lock so that if a jack's hydraulic seal or hose blows out, the 70-tonne aircraft cannot drop onto personnel working underneath
To keep dust off the shiny chrome jack pistons
To ground the aircraft against lightning inside the hangar
explanation: Hydraulic pressure alone is never trusted to support a jacked aircraft. Screwing the heavy threaded safety collars tight against the jack cylinder base mechanically locks the ram against sudden hydraulic failure.

question: In engine oil maintenance, what is the difference between a 'Magnetic Chip Detector' (MCD) and 'SOAP' (Spectrometric Oil Analysis Program)?
options: SOAP is used to wash the outside of the engine cowling

Magnetic Chip Detectors catch larger ferromagnetic iron/steel flakes in the oil scavenge lines, whereas SOAP burns oil samples in a lab spectrometer to measure microscopic wear-metal trends (in ppm) including non-magnetic alloys
Chip detectors only work when the engine is shut down in storage
SOAP measures fuel quantity inside the wing tanks
explanation: MCDs trap macroscopic ferrous slivers from spalling bearings, while SOAP detects sub-microscopic suspended metallic elements (iron, copper, aluminum, silver, chromium) in parts per million to catch wear trends weeks before failure.

question: In aviation Human Factors, what is the core principle of 'Just Culture' inside an airline or MRO?
options: Nobody can ever be disciplined, even for deliberate sabotage or falsifying records
Anyone who makes an honest mistake is fired immediately to set an example

Honest, unintentional human errors and slips that are openly self-reported are protected from punishment so hidden hazards get fixed, while gross negligence or willful violations remain strictly accountable
Only pilots are allowed to report safety issues
explanation: Punishing honest human errors drives mechanics and pilots to hide mistakes. Just Culture encourages immediate self-reporting of honest errors while drawing a clear line against reckless or deliberate rule violations.
source: EASA Part-145 / DGCA CAR-145 Module 9 Human Factors

question: In aviation maintenance Human Factors ('The Dirty Dozen'), why do hangars teach the '3-Steps-Back Rule' whenever a mechanic is interrupted mid-task?
options: So the mechanic stands 3 steps away from the aircraft while talking
Because 'Distraction' is a leading cause of forgotten torque/lockwire steps—backing up 3 full steps in the manual upon returning ensures no un-torqued fastener was mentally skipped
Because mechanics must walk backward around the wingtip
To give the hydraulic fluid 3 minutes to cool down
explanation: When interrupted mid-task, human working memory frequently assumes the current step (like final torquing or lockwiring) was already completed. Re-verifying the last three steps of the procedure defeats distraction lapses.
source: FAA / Transport Canada Human Factors 'Dirty Dozen'

question: According to Bernoulli's Principle in subsonic incompressible airflow, what happens when air accelerates over the curved upper surface of an aerofoil?
options: Static pressure increases and dynamic pressure decreases
Static pressure decreases and dynamic pressure increases
Both static and dynamic pressure increase together
Total pressure drops to zero at the thickest point of the wing
explanation: Total Pressure = Static Pressure + Dynamic Pressure. As airflow velocity increases over the cambered upper surface, dynamic pressure rises and static pressure drops, creating an upward pressure differential (lift).
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 Basic Aerodynamics

question: Why does a symmetric aerofoil (such as a NACA 0012 vertical fin or wind-tunnel test wing) generate zero net lift at a 0-degree Angle of Attack?
options: Because symmetric aerofoils cannot fly faster than 100 knots
Because the upper and lower surfaces have identical curvature, producing equal velocity and equal static pressure on both sides at 0° Angle of Attack
Because boundary-layer air only flows under the wing
Because symmetric aerofoils have no leading edge
explanation: A symmetric aerofoil has zero camber (identical upper and lower profiles). At 0° AoA, airflow accelerates equally over top and bottom surfaces, resulting in zero pressure differential until a positive or negative Angle of Attack is introduced.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 Basic Aerodynamics

question: What happens to the 'Center of Pressure' (CP) on a conventional cambered aerofoil as the Angle of Attack increases toward the stall angle?
options: It stays locked at the trailing edge at all angles
It moves steadily forward toward the leading edge until the critical stall angle is reached, and then shifts abruptly rearward at the stall
It moves sideways out toward the wingtip
It moves steadily backward toward the trailing edge before the stall
explanation: On a cambered wing, the Center of Pressure moves forward as Angle of Attack increases (up to the critical stall angle ~15°–16°), whereas the Aerodynamic Center (AC) remains stationary at roughly the 25% chord point.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 Basic Aerodynamics

question: In aircraft longitudinal stability, what is required for an aircraft to be statically stable in pitch?
options: The Center of Gravity (CG) must be located behind the Center of Lift / Neutral Point
The Center of Gravity (CG) must be located ahead of the Neutral Point (Aerodynamic Center), with the horizontal tailplane providing a balancing downward force
The aircraft must have four engines mounted on the tail
The wings must have negative dihedral (anhedral)
explanation: Positive static longitudinal stability requires a positive 'Static Margin'—meaning the CG sits forward of the Neutral Point so any nose-up gust naturally creates a nose-down restoring pitching moment.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 Basic Aerodynamics

question: Why do modern airliners fit upright Winglets or Sharklets at their wingtips?
options: To act as radio antennas for cabin Wi-Fi
To block high-pressure air under the wing from curling around the tip to the low-pressure upper surface—weakening wingtip vortices and reducing Lift-Induced Drag
To increase Parasite Drag during landing roll
To hold the navigation strobe lights higher off the tarmac
explanation: Winglets and Sharklets diffuse the spanwise flow and strong wingtip vortex where high-pressure lower air spills onto the low-pressure upper wing—increasing effective aspect ratio and cutting induced drag by 3% to 5%.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 Basic Aerodynamics

question: How does 'Induced Drag' (lift-dependent drag) behave vs. 'Parasite Drag' (profile/skin-friction drag) as an aircraft's airspeed increases?
options: Both Induced Drag and Parasite Drag increase with the square of airspeed
Induced Drag is highest at slow speeds (high Angle of Attack) and decreases as speed rises, whereas Parasite Drag increases with the square of airspeed ($V^2$)
Induced Drag is zero during takeoff and maximum at Mach 0.85
Parasite Drag is highest when the aircraft is flying slowly
explanation: Induced drag varies inversely with the square of airspeed ($1/V^2$) because flying slowly requires a high Angle of Attack and strong tip vortices. Parasite drag varies directly with $V^2$. Total drag is lowest where the two curves cross ($L/D_{max}$).
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 Basic Aerodynamics

question: What is the primary aerodynamic difference between extending 'Leading-Edge Slats' vs. 'Trailing-Edge Flaps'?
options: Slats decrease the stall angle while flaps increase it

Leading-edge slats re-energize the upper boundary layer through a slot to increase the Critical Stall Angle ($\alpha_{crit}$), whereas trailing-edge flaps increase camber to boost lift at a given angle
Slats are only used in cruise at 38,000 feet
Flaps reduce wing surface area while slats reduce drag
explanation: Extending leading-edge slats opens a converging slot that ducts high-energy air over the upper wing surface, delaying airflow separation and raising the critical stall angle from ~15° to ~22°–25°.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 Basic Aerodynamics

question: What is 'Adverse Yaw' when an aircraft banks into a turn using its ailerons?
options: The nose yaws in the same direction as the turn too quickly
The downward-moving aileron (on the rising outer wing) creates more lift AND more induced drag than the upward-moving aileron, pulling the aircraft's nose toward the outside of the turn
The rudder pedals lock up above 200 knots
The engines lose thrust during a bank
explanation: When rolling left, the right wing's aileron deflects downward to raise the right wing. That increased local camber produces higher induced drag on the right wingtip, yawing the nose right (away from the left turn) unless countered by differential ailerons, roll spoilers, or rudder.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 Basic Aerodynamics

question: What does 'Critical Mach Number' ($M_{crit}$) mean for a high-speed subsonic airliner?
options: The speed at which the entire aircraft breaks the sound barrier (Mach 1.0)
The lowest flight Mach number at which local airflow accelerating over the thickest part of the wing first reaches the speed of sound (Mach 1.0)
The stall speed when flying with ice on the wings
The maximum speed allowed while taxiing on the ramp
explanation: Because air accelerates as it curves over the upper wing, when the aircraft is flying at Mach 0.78–0.82, local airflow on top of the wing reaches Mach 1.0 first. That free-stream speed is the Critical Mach Number ($M_{crit}$).
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 High Speed Flight

question: Why are the wings of modern commercial jetliners swept backward at roughly 25 to 35 degrees?
options: So the wingtips fit inside narrow airport hangars
To delay the onset of transonic shockwaves and compressibility drag—raising the wing's Critical Mach Number ($M_{crit}$) so the aircraft can cruise efficiently at Mach 0.80+
To increase lift during low-speed landings
To move the fuel tanks behind the tailcone
explanation: Sweeping the wing backward means only the velocity component perpendicular (normal) to the leading edge accelerates over the airfoil camber—delaying shockwave formation and raising $M_{crit}$.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 8 High Speed Flight

question: In CAR-66 Module 3 (Electrical Fundamentals), if three resistors of $30\ \Omega$, $30\ \Omega$, and $30\ \Omega$ are connected in PARALLEL across a 28V DC aircraft bus, what is the total equivalent resistance?
options: 90 Ohms
30 Ohms
10 Ohms
3 Ohms
explanation: For $N$ identical resistors in parallel, $R_{total} = R / N = 30\ \Omega / 3 = 10\ \Omega$. (Total resistance in a parallel circuit is always smaller than the smallest individual branch resistor.)
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 3 Electrical Fundamentals

question: In an Alternating Current (AC) circuit, what is the phase relationship between Voltage and Current across a pure Inductor vs. a pure Capacitor?
options: Voltage and current are always in phase in both
