In an Inductor, Voltage leads Current by 90° (ELI); in a Capacitor, Current leads Voltage by 90° (ICE)
In an Inductor, Current leads Voltage by 90°; in a Capacitor, Voltage leads Current by 90°
Voltage lags Current by 180° in both
explanation: Remember the classic aviation mnemonic 'ELI the ICE man': in an Inductive (L) circuit, EMF (Voltage, E) leads Current (I) by 90°; in a Capacitive (C) circuit, Current (I) leads EMF (E) by 90°.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 3 AC Theory

question: Why are aircraft AC generators rated in 'kVA' (Kilovolt-Amperes, Apparent Power) such as 90 kVA, rather than in 'kW' (Kilowatts, True Power)?
options: Because kVA sounds larger in marketing brochures

Because generator copper windings and iron cores are thermally limited by total current ($V \times I$) regardless of the Power Factor ($\cos \phi$) of the inductive/capacitive aircraft loads connected
Because 400 Hz electricity has no watts
Because kW only applies to DC batteries
explanation: Internal $I^2R$ heating inside a generator's windings depends on total current flowing, which includes reactive current from inductive motors and transformers. Rating in kVA (Apparent Power) defines the true thermal/current limit independent of load Power Factor.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 3 AC Generators

question: In a 3-Phase Star-Connected (Wye) aircraft AC generator where the Phase Voltage (line-to-neutral) is 115V AC, what is the Line Voltage (phase-to-phase)?
options: 115V AC
200V AC ($115\text{V} \times \sqrt{3}$)
230V AC ($115\text{V} \times 2$)
400V AC
explanation: In a 3-phase Star (Wye) system, Line Voltage equals $\sqrt{3}$ (approx. 1.732) times Phase Voltage: $115\text{V} \times 1.732 \approx 200\text{V}$ AC.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 3 Three-Phase AC

question: Why do Jet Engine EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) thermocouple harnesses use 'Chromel-Alumel' (Type K) wires that must NEVER be trimmed shorter by a mechanic if the wire is too long?
options: Because cutting the wire releases toxic gas
Because thermocouple lead harnesses are calibrated to a specific loop resistance (e.g., 8 Ohms); shortening the wire changes its resistance and causes the cockpit EGT gauge to read inaccurately
Because Chromel wire is hollow and filled with mercury
Because thermocouple wires carry 115V AC power
explanation: Thermocouples generate a tiny millivolt signal via the Seebeck effect where two dissimilar metals (Chromel and Alumel) join. In resistance-calibrated EGT circuits, cutting or splicing the lead alters loop resistance and corrupts temperature accuracy.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 3 & ATA 77 Thermocouples

question: In CAR-66 Module 4 (Electronic Fundamentals), how is a 'Zener Diode' connected in an aircraft voltage regulator circuit, and how does it work?
options: Forward-biased in series to block all current
Reverse-biased across the load; once reverse voltage reaches its precise Zener Breakdown Voltage, it conducts cleanly to clamp and hold voltage constant
Connected to the antenna to amplify VHF radio waves
Used as a mechanical fuse that melts when overloaded
explanation: Unlike normal rectifier diodes that are destroyed by reverse breakdown, a Zener diode is engineered to operate in reverse bias—maintaining a rock-steady reference voltage across its terminals even as input current fluctuates.

question: What component do aircraft flight control actuators and landing gear proximity sensors use to convert linear mechanical movement into a proportional AC electrical signal (LVDT)?
options: A carbon-pile resistor
A Linear Variable Differential Transformer (LVDT) with a movable ferromagnetic core sliding inside one primary and two secondary coils
A glass mercury tilt switch
A pitot tube
explanation: An LVDT uses a frictionless magnetic core attached to the actuator rod moving inside a cylindrical transformer. The phase and amplitude difference between the two secondary windings gives exact position feedback with zero mechanical contact wear.

question: In CAR-66 Module 5 (Digital Techniques), which digital logic gate outputs a '1' (HIGH) ONLY when ALL of its inputs are '1' (HIGH)—commonly used in aircraft safety interlocks like Cargo Smoke dual-loop confirmation?
options: OR Gate
AND Gate
XOR (Exclusive-OR) Gate
NOT Gate (Inverter)
explanation: An AND gate produces a HIGH (1) output only if Input A AND Input B are both HIGH (1). Aircraft warning computers use AND logic when two independent sensors (e.g., Loop A + Loop B) must agree before triggering an action.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 5 Logic Gates

question: What is the key architectural difference between an 'ARINC 429' data bus (used on A320/B737) and an 'ARINC 629 / AFDX' data bus (used on B777/A380/A350/B787)?
options: ARINC 429 uses fiber-optic lasers while AFDX uses pneumatic tubes
ARINC 429 is a unidirectional (one-way) twisted-shielded pair where only ONE transmitter can talk to up to 20 receivers per wire pair, whereas ARINC 629 / AFDX are high-speed bi-directional networks
ARINC 429 can carry 115V AC power to run hydraulic pumps
AFDX only works on the ground when connected to airport Wi-Fi
explanation: ARINC 429 is a rock-solid unidirectional 32-bit bus (one talker, up to 20 listeners per twisted shielded pair—meaning two boxes talking back and forth require two separate wire pairs), while AFDX is a deterministic bi-directional switched Ethernet network.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 5 Data Buses

question: Why must an avionics engineer wear a grounded 'ESD Wrist Strap' (containing a 1-megaohm safety resistor) before pulling a circuit card or touching an open Line Replaceable Unit (LRU)?
options: To keep the engineer's hands warm in the avionics bay
Because static electricity on a human body (even an unfelt 100-volt discharge) can punch through microscopic CMOS microchip gate oxides—causing immediate or latent in-flight failure
To boost the engineer's flashlight battery
To prevent the LRU from falling off the rack
explanation: Humans don't even feel an Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) below ~3,000 volts, yet sensitive avionics microchips can be degraded by as little as 20–100 volts. The wrist strap bleeds static safely to ground through a 1 M$\Omega$ current-limiting resistor.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 5 ESD Protection

question: In an aircraft's 24-bit ICAO Mode S Transponder address (and computer memory), why do avionics engineers represent binary numbers in 'Hexadecimal' (Base-16, using 0–9 and A–F)?
options: Because computers cannot read ones and zeros
Because every single Hexadecimal digit compactly represents exactly 4 binary bits (a 'nibble'), turning a clumsy 24-bit binary string into a clean 6-character code
Because Hexadecimal uses less electrical power
Because pilots only have 16 buttons on the transponder keypad
explanation: Since $2^4 = 16$, four binary bits map directly to one hexadecimal character (e.g., `1111` = `F`, `1010` = `A`). This allows a 24-bit ICAO aircraft address to be written cleanly as 6 hex characters (e.g., `800B4A`).
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 5 Numbering Systems

question: In aviation aluminum alloys (CAR-66 Module 6), what is the primary alloying element and typical use of '2024' series vs. '7075' series aluminum?
options: 2024 uses lead for ballast; 7075 uses tin for soldering

2024 is alloyed with Copper (~4.4%) for high damage-tolerance/fracture toughness (fuselage & lower wing skins), while 7075 is alloyed with Zinc (~5.6%) for maximum ultimate strength (upper wing skins & spars)
Both are 100% pure unalloyed aluminum
2024 is magnetic steel and 7075 is titanium
explanation: 2000-series (Al-Copper, like 2024-T3) excels in tension and crack-growth resistance (damage-tolerant fuselage/lower wing skin), while 7000-series (Al-Zinc, like 7075-T6) provides higher compressive/ultimate strength for upper wing skins and frames.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 6 Aircraft Materials

question: What is 'Alclad' sheet metal used on aircraft fuselage skins?
options: Aluminum painted with black radar-absorbing paint
A high-strength alloy core (such as 2024 or 7075) sandwich-rolled with a thin surface layer of pure aluminum on both sides to protect the core against corrosion
A mixture of carbon fiber and fiberglass
Stainless steel bolts dipped in liquid nitrogen
explanation: Alloying aluminum with copper (2024) or zinc (7075) makes it strong but susceptible to intergranular corrosion. Pure aluminum is soft but highly corrosion-resistant—so bonding a thin 5% pure aluminum skin ('Alclad') onto both faces gives the best of both worlds.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 6 Ferrous & Non-Ferrous Materials

question: Why cannot bare Carbon-Fiber Reinforced Plastic (CFRP) composite panels be fastened directly against bare aluminum ribs using aluminum rivets without an insulating fiberglass/sealant barrier?
options: Because aluminum rivets are too heavy for carbon fiber
Because carbon is electrically noble (cathodic) and aluminum is anodic—touching them together in moisture creates a powerful galvanic battery that rapidly corrodes and dissolves the aluminum!
Because carbon fiber melts when touched by aluminum
Because aluminum rivets are magnetic
explanation: On the galvanic series, graphite/carbon fiber sits near gold and platinum, while aluminum sits at the active anodic end. Direct contact between CFRP and aluminum causes rapid galvanic corrosion of the aluminum unless titanium/Inconel fasteners and a fiberglass barrier ply are used.
source: DGCA / EASA CAR-66 Module 6 Composites & Corrosion

question: How does a 'Hi-Lok' (or Hi-Lite) structural fastener ensure the exact correct preload torque is applied to a wing or fuselage joint during installation?
options: The mechanic counts exactly 12 turns with a hand screwdriver
Its threaded collar has a precision machined 'shear groove'—when tightened with an Allen key and socket, the hex driving hex-head snaps off automatically at the exact calibrated preload torque
It is welded in place with an oxy-acetylene torch
It uses a rubber band inside the nut
explanation: A Hi-Lok pin is held from rotating with an Allen hex key while the self-locking collar is driven down until its calibrated frangible hex nut shears off cleanly at the predetermined torque.

question: What does 'AOG' stand for in airline maintenance and logistics?
options: Airbus Operations Group
Aircraft On Ground
Approved Overhaul Guide
Automated Oil Gauge
explanation: Aircraft On Ground (AOG) is the highest-priority emergency status in aviation logistics, indicating an aircraft is grounded by a technical defect and unable to fly revenue service until a part or repair arrives.

question: What does 'CAMO' stand for under EASA and DGCA regulatory frameworks?
options: Commercial Airline Maintenance Office
Continuing Airworthiness Management Organisation
Certified Aircraft Modification Operator
Central Avionics Monitoring Output
explanation: A Continuing Airworthiness Management Organisation (CAMO) is the approved organization responsible for managing an aircraft's maintenance programme, AD/SB compliance, technical records, and airworthiness reviews.

question: What does 'ARC' stand for in continuing airworthiness documentation?
options: Aircraft Repair Checklist
Airworthiness Review Certificate
Authorized Replacement Component
Automatic Rudder Control
explanation: The Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC, Form 15a/b/c) is the 12-month certificate validating that an aircraft's Certificate of Airworthiness remains currently valid following a records and physical audit.

question: What does 'CRS' stand for when a licensed engineer signs off a maintenance job in the Technical Log?
options: Component Repair Sheet
Certificate of Release to Service
Cabin Readiness Status
Continuous Recording System
explanation: A Certificate of Release to Service (CRS) is the legal certification signed by appropriately authorized Part-145 / CAR-145 staff confirming that maintenance was completed in accordance with approved data.

question: What does 'LLP' stand for in jet engine and landing gear technical records?
options: Low Level Pressure
Life-Limited Part
Longitudinal Load Pin
Line Lubrication Procedure
explanation: A Life-Limited Part (LLP) is a critical rotor or structural part with a mandatory hard replacement limit (usually in Flight Cycles) published in the Airworthiness Limitations Section, requiring full Back-to-Birth traceability.

question: In a CAMO maintenance due list, what does 'LDND' stand for?
options: Landing Distance Not Determined
Last Done / Next Due
Low Density Nitrogen Discharge
Line Defect Notification Document
explanation: LDND (Last Done / Next Due) is the master maintenance status tracking sheet showing when every AMP/MPD task, hard-time component, and repetitive AD was last accomplished (FH/FC/Date) and when it falls next due.

question: In technical records, what do 'TSO' and 'CSO' stand for on an overhauled rotable component?
options: Technical Service Order and Cabin Safety Officer
Time Since Overhaul and Cycles Since Overhaul
Total System Output and Current Switch Open
Turbine Shaft Oil and Compressor Seal Oil
explanation: While TSN/CSN measure Time and Cycles Since New (from factory birth), TSO and CSO measure the Flight Hours and Flight Cycles accumulated since the component's last zero-time shop Overhaul.

question: What does 'MPD' stand for in aircraft maintenance planning?
options: Maximum Pressure Differential
Maintenance Planning Document
Main Power Distribution
Mechanical Pump Drive
explanation: Published by the airframe OEM (derived from the Maintenance Review Board Report / MRBR), the Maintenance Planning Document (MPD) provides all baseline scheduled maintenance tasks and intervals used to build an airline's AMP.

question: What does 'SRM' stand for when evaluating a fuselage skin dent?
options: System Reset Manual
Structural Repair Manual
Safety Risk Management
Stabilizer Rigging Manual
explanation: The Structural Repair Manual (SRM) is the OEM-approved manual defining allowable structural damage limits (dents, scratches, corrosion) and standard pre-approved sheet-metal/composite repair schemes.

question: What does 'CMM' stand for inside an off-aircraft component overhaul shop (and in Block 12 of an EASA Form 1)?
options: Cabin Maintenance Manual
Component Maintenance Manual
Central Monitoring Module
Continuous Metal Measurement
explanation: While line and base mechanics working on the aircraft use the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual), back-shop technicians overhauling an unbolted valve or pump on the bench must use the OEM's Component Maintenance Manual (CMM).

question: What does 'LOPA' stand for in aircraft cabin engineering and transitions?
options: Low Oil Pressure Alarm
Layout of Passenger Accommodations
Landing Overweight Performance Assessment
List of Approved Parts and Assemblies
explanation: The LOPA (Layout of Passenger Accommodations) is the certified engineering blueprint drawing of the aircraft cabin showing exact seat row pitches, seat part numbers, galleys, lavatories, and emergency equipment locations.

question: What does 'NDT' (or 'NDI') stand for in structural maintenance?
options: Nose Door Trim
Non-Destructive Testing (or Non-Destructive Inspection)
Nitrogen Drain Tube
Normal Takeoff Distance
explanation: Non-Destructive Testing (Eddy Current, Ultrasonic, Magnetic Particle, Liquid Penetrant, Radiography) evaluates subsurface and surface flaws without harming the part's serviceability.

question: What does 'FOD' stand for on an airport ramp or inside a maintenance hangar?
options: Flight Operations Director
Foreign Object Debris (or Foreign Object Damage)
Fuel Overfill Drain
Forward Overhead Door
explanation: FOD refers both to any loose object, tool, stone, or hardware that doesn't belong in the environment (Foreign Object Debris) and the resulting damage if ingested by an engine or jammed in controls (Foreign Object Damage).

question: What does 'RAT' stand for in an aircraft emergency electrical/hydraulic system?
options: Rudder Actuator Trim
Ram Air Turbine
Radar Altimeter Transceiver
Reserve Auxiliary Tank
explanation: The Ram Air Turbine (RAT) is a small drop-down wind turbine that deploys into the slipstream to generate emergency hydraulic pressure and/or electrical power if main power sources are lost.

question: What does 'BITE' stand for when troubleshooting an avionics computer fault?
options: Brake Indicator Temperature Equipment
Built-In Test Equipment
Basic Instrument Training Exam
Battery Inverter Thermal Element
explanation: Built-In Test Equipment (BITE) refers to the automated internal fault-detection and self-diagnostic circuits/software built inside modern avionics LRUs and accessed via the cockpit MCDU/CMC.

question: What does 'TCAS' (or 'ACAS') stand for?
options: Turbine Cooling Air System
Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (Airborne Collision Avoidance System)
Thermal Cabin Air Sensor
Takeoff Climb Attitude System
explanation: TCAS (the hardware implementation of ICAO's ACAS standard) interrogates nearby Mode S/C transponders to issue Traffic Advisories (TAs) and vertical Resolution Advisories (RAs).

question: What does 'RVSM' stand for in high-altitude airspace between FL290 and FL410?
options: Rudder Vertical Stabilizer Mechanism
Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum
Radar Velocity Speed Monitor
Regional Visual Approach Minimum
explanation: RVSM reduces required vertical separation between IFR aircraft from 2,000 feet down to 1,000 feet between 29,000 ft (FL290) and 41,000 ft (FL410) for certified aircraft with high-precision altimetry.

question: What does 'ETOPS' stand for under modern ICAO and EASA definitions?
options: Engine Thrust Over-Pressure System
Extended Diversion Time Operations (historically Extended-range Twin-engine Operational Performance Standards)
Emergency Takeoff Power Setting
Electronic Transponder Operating System
explanation: Originally coined for twin-engine overwater flights ('Engines Turn Or Passengers Swim' in pilot humor!), ETOPS stands for Extended Diversion Time Operations beyond the baseline 60-minute threshold.

question: In aircraft weight and balance, what do 'MTOW', 'MLW', and 'MZFW' stand for?
options: Main Tyre Outer Width, Main Leg Weight, and Minimum Zone Fuel Weight
Maximum Takeoff Weight, Maximum Landing Weight, and Maximum Zero Fuel Weight
Mean Turbine Operating Wattage, Minimum Lift Weight, and Main Zone Firewall
Manual Throttle Override Wheel, Manual Landing Wheel, and Master Zero Fuel Warning
explanation: These are the three primary structural weight ceilings of an aircraft: Maximum Zero Fuel Weight (wing-root bending limit before fuel), Maximum Takeoff Weight, and Maximum Landing Weight.

question: On a Load and Trim Sheet, why is the Center of Gravity (CG) expressed as '% MAC' (e.g., 27% MAC), and what does MAC stand for?
options: Maximum Air Conditioning
Mean Aerodynamic Chord—the average chord length of a tapered/swept wing, providing a universal reference scale for where the balance point sits relative to the wing's lift
Minimum Approach Climb
Main Avionics Computer
explanation: Because swept wings taper from root to tip, engineers define the Mean Aerodynamic Chord (MAC)—a reference chord representing the aerodynamic average of the whole wing—and express CG as a percentage from the leading edge of the MAC.
source: ATA 08 / Aircraft Weight and Balance Manual

question: Which ATA chapter covers Indicating and Recording Systems (including cockpit displays, Flight Warning Computers, DFDR, and QAR)?
options: ATA 23
ATA 31
ATA 34
ATA 49
explanation: ATA 31 covers Indicating and Recording Systems (EIS displays, Flight Warning Computers, clocks, Flight Data Recorders, and Quick Access Recorders).

question: Which ATA chapter covers Standard Practices – Airframe (including torque values, lockwiring, fluid line fittings, and EWIS electrical wiring practices)?
options: ATA 05
ATA 12
ATA 20
ATA 51
explanation: ATA 20 covers Standard Practices – Airframe (fastener torque, safety wiring, fluid tubes, bonding, and EWIS), whereas ATA 51 covers Standard Practices – Structures (riveting, sheet metal, and corrosion).

question: Which ATA chapter covers Time Limits / Maintenance Checks (including scheduled checks AND unscheduled conditional inspections like Hard Landing, Bird Strike, and Lightning Strike)?
options: ATA 05
ATA 10
ATA 20
ATA 32
explanation: ATA 05 covers Time Limits and Maintenance Checks—including Sub-chapter 05-51 Unscheduled / Conditional Maintenance Checks after hard landings, severe turbulence, lightning strikes, or bird strikes.

question: Which ATA chapter covers Parking, Mooring, Storage and Return to Service (the chapter used when preserving an aircraft in a desert storage facility)?
options: ATA 07
ATA 08
ATA 09
ATA 10
explanation: ATA 10 covers Parking, Mooring, Storage and Return to Service. (ATA 07 is Lifting/Shoring, ATA 08 is Leveling/Weighing, and ATA 09 is Towing/Taxiing.)
ataTitle: Parking, Mooring, Storage and Return to Service

question: Which ATA chapter covers Power Plant (the complete engine QEC package, cowlings, engine mounts, and drains) vs. ATA 72 (the internal turbine engine core & modules)?
options: ATA 49
ATA 71
ATA 75
ATA 79
explanation: ATA 71 is Power Plant (covering the external QEC installation, fan/reverser cowlings, mounts, and engine change procedures), while ATA 72 covers the internal Turbine/Turboprop Engine modules.
